paragraphs: This paper develops an accelerated randomized approach to solving linear systems, with matrix inversion as an important application. Rather than treating inversion only as a calculation performed once, the approach builds successive approximations. For positive definite matrices, the algorithm can preserve positive definiteness at every step, so intermediate approximations retain a structural property useful in optimization.

The authors use this general framework to construct accelerated quasi-Newton updates, including both deterministic and stochastic versions. These updates approximate the inverse Hessian, the matrix describing how an objective's curvature should influence an optimization step. The theoretical contribution is that the new updates produce provably more aggressive inverse-Hessian approximations, connecting accelerated linear algebra with the rules used to train models.

Numerical experiments show speed improvements over classical updates without acceleration. Experiments on empirical risk minimization also show that the proposed rules can accelerate machine-learning training. Together, these findings support the practical value of the theory, while the training improvement remains an experimental finding rather than a guarantee for every model.
neurips-2018-accelerated-stochastic-matr.tldr: Accelerated randomized linear-system methods yield structure-preserving matrix inversion and quasi-Newton updates that can speed model training.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an image from measurements, as in denoising or medical imaging. A regularizer helps guide reconstruction by expressing which candidate images are preferable. This paper proposes learning that regularizer with a neural network, bringing information from image data into the variational optimization framework traditionally used for these problems.

The network learns to distinguish the distribution of ground-truth images from the distribution of reconstructions produced without regularization. This discrimination task supplies a learned criterion for assessing reconstructed images. After training, the network becomes the regularization functional in the corresponding variational problem, and solving that problem produces the reconstruction. The learned component therefore participates directly in the reconstruction objective.

An important feature is that the framework can operate with unsupervised training data, broadening the circumstances in which learned regularization can be used. Experiments address image denoising on BSDS and computed tomography reconstruction on LIDC. These results demonstrate the framework's potential across two reconstruction tasks, supporting the idea that distribution-based learning can improve the guidance supplied to an inverse-problem solver.
neurips-2018-adversarial-regularizers-in.tldr: A neural network learns an image regularizer from distributions and then guides variational reconstruction, even with unsupervised training data.

paragraphs: Clicks are plentiful, but they do not directly reveal how users evaluate every result they are shown. Feedback depends both on whether a user examines a result and on whether they judge it relevant. This paper addresses that ambiguity in contextual bandit learning, where the system must choose actions while learning from the feedback those choices generate.

The proposed model explicitly separates examination from relevance judgment. Because examination is unobserved, it is represented using latent variables rather than treated as directly available evidence. Variational Bayesian inference supports learning in this model, while Thompson sampling selects actions. Together, these components connect uncertainty about hidden user behavior with the system's ongoing decisions and model updates.

The authors derive an upper bound on regret, providing theoretical support for learning from implicit feedback in this setting. They also evaluate the method using click logs from a major online-course platform and report effective learning in practice. The central contribution is a decision-making method that accounts for why feedback is incomplete, rather than interpreting each observed response as an unambiguous relevance judgment.
neurips-2018-bandit-learning-with-implic.tldr: Separating hidden examination behavior from relevance judgments enables contextual bandit learning from ambiguous click feedback.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of two unknown signals from Fourier measurements of their circular convolution when phase information is missing. Both signals may be real or complex. The challenge combines disentangling the two inputs with recovering information absent from the measurements, so the observations do not directly expose either original signal.

The proposed method reformulates the task as matrix recovery and then constructs a convex relaxation of the measurements' bilinear structure. This produces a computationally efficient approach with a theoretical recovery guarantee. It also avoids requiring an initial estimate of the solution, making the guarantee independent of first finding a suitable starting reconstruction.

The guarantee assumes that the signals lie in known random subspaces of dimensions k and n, and requires m to be sufficiently larger than (k+n) log² m. Recovery is only up to the problem's inherent scaling ambiguity. The proof uses Rademacher complexity estimates, and the authors provide an ADMM implementation with numerical experiments supporting the theory. These conditions specify the setting in which the recovery claim applies.
neurips-2018-blind-deconvolutional-phase.tldr: A convex matrix-recovery method provably reconstructs two convolved signals from phaseless measurements under known random-subspace assumptions.

paragraphs: Deep generative models can produce rich outputs, but incorporating structured domain knowledge into their training is difficult. Posterior regularization offers a way to impose constraints on probabilistic models. Its traditional formulation, however, fits poorly with generators that lack a Bayesian interpretation or explicit density evaluation, and it requires constraints to be specified completely before learning.

This paper establishes a mathematical connection between posterior regularization and reinforcement learning. Using that connection, it treats learnable constraints as an external reward. The generator and the uncertain parts of its knowledge constraints can then adapt jointly. This matters when useful knowledge has structure but cannot realistically be written down as a fully fixed set of requirements.

The resulting algorithm is presented as model-agnostic and applicable across deep generative models, with flexibility to accommodate arbitrary constraints. Experiments on human-image generation and sentence generation from templates report substantial improvements over the underlying generative models. The findings support learning how to apply domain knowledge alongside learning to generate outputs, instead of requiring every aspect of that knowledge to be settled beforehand.
neurips-2018-deep-generative-models-with.tldr: A connection between posterior regularization and reinforcement learning lets generative models learn knowledge constraints jointly with their outputs.

paragraphs: Conversational questions often leave information unstated because earlier turns already supplied it. This paper addresses that problem by translating each utterance into a logical form that can be executed against a large knowledge base. Understanding a question therefore involves constructing an explicit query while recovering the context needed to make that query meaningful.

The approach maintains dialog memory containing earlier entities, predicates, and logical forms. A generative model uses this history while interpreting the current utterance, building its logical form from the top down according to a small, flexible grammar. Remembering previous query structure alongside the things being discussed gives the model resources for resolving the omissions common in conversation.

Training uses denotations, or the answers produced by logical forms, without requiring explicit annotations of those forms. Evaluation covers 200,000 dialogs involving 12.8 million entities. The reported results support the benefits of dialog memory and show a large advantage over a memory-network encoder-decoder model. The contribution combines contextual conversation handling with executable semantic structure at the scale of a large knowledge base.
neurips-2018-dialog-to-action-conversati.tldr: Dialog memory helps a semantic parser turn context-dependent conversational questions into executable knowledge-base queries.

paragraphs: Symmetric nonnegative matrix factorization is useful for data analysis, particularly clustering, but its symmetry makes efficient optimization difficult. General nonsymmetric factorization permits splitting the problem into parts that can be updated alternately. This paper seeks to bring that computational advantage to the symmetric problem without giving up the connection to its original solutions.

The authors construct a nonsymmetric reformulation and rigorously establish that solving it returns a solution for symmetric factorization. They then adapt fast alternating optimization ideas from nonsymmetric NMF. The important move is to change the formulation used during computation, allowing efficient updates while retaining a mathematical relationship to the symmetric task.

The resulting algorithms have convergence guarantees for the generated sequence: convergence occurs at least at a sublinear rate, and the sequence converges globally to a critical point of symmetric NMF. A critical point is not necessarily a globally optimal solution, so the guarantee concerns convergence rather than universal optimality. Experiments with synthetic data and image clustering support the proposed reformulation and optimization approach.
neurips-2018-dropping-symmetry-for-fast-.tldr: A nonsymmetric reformulation enables fast alternating algorithms for symmetric NMF with convergence guarantees to a critical point.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents must explore actions to discover good behavior, but exploration of inferior actions incurs regret. This paper studies finite state and action spaces where the underlying decision process has known structure. The central question is how that structure can reduce the exploration needed to distinguish useful choices from suboptimal ones.

The authors derive problem-specific regret lower bounds for arbitrary structure and make them explicit for unstructured and Lipschitz decision processes. In the Lipschitz case, transition probabilities and average rewards vary in a controlled way across states and actions. The resulting lower bounds are below c log T, with c determined by structural properties, the bias-function span, and the smallest action gap, rather than directly by state and action counts.

For unstructured problems, the lower bound typically scales as SA log T. The authors introduce Directed Exploration Learning, which matches their bounds, and give a simplified Lipschitz version that still exploits structure efficiently. The result links the information required for exploration to an algorithm that attains the corresponding regret bounds.
neurips-2018-exploration-in-structured-r.tldr: Problem-specific regret bounds and Directed Exploration Learning show how known structure can reduce reinforcement-learning exploration costs.

paragraphs: Genetic-Gated Networks add a vector of binary genetic genes to one or more hidden layers of a neural network. These genes act as gates, providing a discrete way to vary the model alongside its trainable neural parameters. The design creates a setting in which genetic search and gradient-based learning can both contribute to optimization.

The motivation is that the two forms of optimization have complementary strengths. Gradient-free methods can be effective when a problem contains multiple local minima, while gradient-based methods can find a local minimum quickly. G2N combines these capabilities in a simple network design. Different chromosomes can also define different models, making it easier to construct multiple models for tasks that benefit from having them.

The authors apply G2N to typical reinforcement-learning algorithms and report large improvements in sample efficiency and performance. Better sample efficiency means learning more effectively from the experience collected during training. The stated result supports binary genetic gating as a useful addition to reinforcement-learning networks, while describing improvements observed in the applications rather than guaranteeing them for every learning problem.
neurips-2018-genetic-gated-networks-for-.tldr: Binary genetic gates combine gradient-free search with gradient-based learning and improve sample efficiency and performance in reinforcement-learning applications.

paragraphs: Training on a distributed computing system requires balancing work performed on individual machines against communication between them. GIANT addresses this balance for empirical risk minimization using a Newton-type optimization method. Its purpose is to exploit curvature information while keeping the coordination required across workers efficient.

At each iteration, every worker computes a local approximate Newton direction and sends it to a central driver. The driver averages these directions to form the global GIANT direction. The method exposes a useful trade-off: doing more computation locally can reduce the total number of communication rounds. This makes local effort part of the strategy for improving distributed optimization, rather than focusing solely on the cost of each iteration.

The authors prove an improved convergence rate relative to first-order methods and existing distributed Newton-type methods considered in their analysis. They also emphasize that GIANT has only one tuning parameter, simplifying its practical configuration. Large-scale experiments on a computer cluster report superior performance, providing empirical support for combining local approximate curvature calculations through a simple global average.
neurips-2018-giant-globally-improved-app.tldr: GIANT averages workers' approximate Newton directions to accelerate distributed optimization while trading local computation for fewer communication rounds.

paragraphs: Generating useful molecules requires more than producing plausible graphs. A system must pursue desired properties while respecting chemical rules such as valency. Some objectives and rules are complex or non-differentiable, making them difficult to incorporate directly into ordinary gradient-based generation. This paper frames the task as goal-directed graph generation through reinforcement learning.

The Graph Convolutional Policy Network uses a graph convolutional model to guide generation. Policy-gradient training combines domain-specific rewards with an adversarial loss, while the environment incorporates domain-specific rules. This arrangement gives property optimization and rule compliance explicit roles in the generation process. In the molecular application, it also allows the system to pursue improvements while producing structures resembling known molecules.

The experiments report a 61% improvement in chemical-property optimization over state-of-the-art baselines and a 184% improvement on constrained property optimization. These are results for the evaluated tasks, rather than guarantees about every generated molecule. They support the broader proposal that reinforcement learning can coordinate graph-based generation, complex objectives, and structural requirements within one model.
neurips-2018-graph-convolutional-policy-.tldr: GCPN uses reinforcement learning to generate molecular graphs that optimize target properties while operating under domain-specific rules.

paragraphs: This paper examines why deep ReLU networks can fail at the beginning of training. It separates two problems involving activation length: an average magnitude that explodes or vanishes, and a variance that becomes exponentially large. Distinguishing these failures matters because controlling the average alone does not automatically control variability in every architecture.

The authors prove that the first failure can be avoided using symmetric weight initialization with variance 2/fan-in, together with appropriate scaling of residual modules in residual networks. Once this first problem is avoided, they prove that the second failure does not occur in residual networks. Fully connected networks behave differently: their variance problem can occur, and avoiding it requires keeping the sum of reciprocal layer widths constant.

The study provides rigorous conditions across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures, then tests how well the theory predicts whether training can begin successfully. The experiments support those predictions. Many popular initialization choices fail the proposed criteria, while suitable initialization and architecture permit much deeper networks to train, making network shape and starting weights jointly important.
neurips-2018-how-to-start-training-the-e.tldr: The paper identifies two early-training failures in deep ReLU networks and proves how initialization and architecture can prevent them.

paragraphs: A network's Lipschitz constant describes how strongly its output can change relative to a change in its input. Estimating it helps assess sensitivity to small perturbations. This paper shows that computing the constant exactly is NP-hard even for two-layer networks, and that existing estimation methods can substantially overestimate it.

The authors introduce AutoLip, a generic method for upper-bounding the Lipschitz constant of automatically differentiable functions. An accompanying power-method algorithm uses automatic differentiation to make calculations efficient even for large convolutions. For sequential networks, SeqLip exploits the linear arrangement of layers and divides the calculation across consecutive layer pairs, using more of the network's structure.

Additional SeqLip heuristics address very large networks, and experiments show that SeqLip can substantially tighten existing upper bounds. The authors also provide an AutoLip implementation in PyTorch. More precise estimates may help assess robustness or regularize a network, but the work also demonstrates the underlying difficulty of obtaining such estimates. Its contribution is better tractable estimation alongside a clear computational barrier to exact calculation.
neurips-2018-lipschitz-regularity-of-dee.tldr: AutoLip and SeqLip improve practical Lipschitz estimation while the paper proves that exact computation is hard even for shallow networks.

paragraphs: Continuous classification of audio or gesture streams can overwhelm tiny devices because a large model must repeatedly process long, overlapping windows. This paper exploits two observations about typical applications: the distinctive signal for a class occupies only a small part of the data, and it can often be recognized early.

EMI-RNN combines a multiple-instance learning formulation with early prediction to use those properties. The approach focuses learning on class signatures while reducing the computation needed before issuing a prediction. On a gesture benchmark, the authors report an accuracy improvement of up to 1% over a standard LSTM while using 72 times less computation. This demonstrates a substantial efficiency gain in that evaluated setting.

The savings enable continuous real-time prediction on small devices, including Raspberry Pi Zero and Arduino variants, where the baseline LSTM could not achieve that task. The paper also analyzes its multiple-instance learning algorithm in a simple setting, proving linear-rate convergence to a global optimum there. That theoretical result applies to the analyzed setting, alongside the empirical evidence for practical sequential classification.
neurips-2018-multiple-instance-learning-.tldr: EMI-RNN combines multiple-instance learning and early prediction to make continuous sequence classification practical on tiny devices.

paragraphs: Dynamic assortment selection concerns choosing which items to offer over time while learning how to earn revenue. This paper studies the problem under an uncapacitated multinomial-logit model, so its result concerns that particular choice model without a capacity restriction on the assortment. Performance is measured by regret, the revenue lost relative to the relevant optimal policy.

The authors analyze a revenue potential function and use that analysis to justify an algorithm based on trisection. The proof combines ideas from unimodal and convex bandit problems with adaptive confidence parameters from minimax multi-armed bandit analysis. These tools connect the structure of the revenue objective with how the algorithm manages uncertainty during repeated choices.

The resulting regret bound is O(√(T log log T)) and does not depend on the number of items. It matches information-theoretic lower bounds up to iterated logarithmic factors, making the policy near-optimal in the stated sense. The notable finding is that, under this model, the guarantee can avoid an explicit item-count penalty while remaining close to the fundamental regret limit.
neurips-2018-near-optimal-policies-for-d.tldr: A trisection-based assortment policy achieves item-independent regret close to the information-theoretic limit under an uncapacitated MNL model.

paragraphs: This paper asks how general a neural network's layers are across a family of related tasks. It introduces a measurement technique based on singular vector canonical correlation analysis, or SVCCA, for tasks that vary continuously with parameters. The aim is to identify representations shared across problems and distinguish them from representations specific to individual tasks.

The authors study networks solving parameterized boundary-value problems based on the Poisson partial differential equation. They find that early hidden layers learn general representations resembling generalized coordinates over the input domain. Later layers become progressively more task-specific. This gives a concrete account of how shared and specialized representations appear within the networks studied.

To validate the measurement, the authors compare it with an existing approach based on transfer-learning experiments. The two methods agree closely, while the proposed technique is much faster, especially for continuously parameterized problems. An additional MNIST application is consistent with and complements another study of intrinsic dimensionality. The contribution therefore includes both a tool for measuring generality and evidence about where general representations arise.
neurips-2018-neural-networks-trained-to-.tldr: An SVCCA-based measure finds general early-layer representations and increasingly specialized deeper layers in networks solving parameterized differential equations.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer preferences from behavior, but behavior reflects both what an agent wants and how it plans. When the agent's degree of rationality is unknown, those two contributions become difficult to separate. This paper studies that general ambiguity rather than assuming a particular, already specified form of human planning error.

The authors show that a No Free Lunch result rules out uniquely decomposing an observed policy into a planning algorithm and a reward function. Observing the policy in additional environments does not resolve this ambiguity. They further show that a reasonable preference for simpler explanations cannot reliably distinguish the true decomposition from alternative decompositions that lead to high regret.

The implication is that simplicity and behavioral observations alone do not supply everything needed for preference inference in this setting. The authors argue that simple normative assumptions are required: assumptions about how behavior should be interpreted that cannot be derived exclusively from observations. The result identifies a foundational obstacle to learning human preferences when planning behavior itself remains unrestricted or unknown.
neurips-2018-occam-s-razor-is-insufficie.tldr: Behavior and a reasonable simplicity prior cannot uniquely identify an agent's preferences when its planning process is unknown.

paragraphs: Learning algorithms optimize empirical risk measured on available data, while the quantity of interest is population risk. Sampling can introduce shallow local minima that belong only to the empirical objective. This paper asks how an algorithm can avoid those misleading minima and find approximate local minima of the underlying population objective.

The analysis assumes a smooth, nonconvex population function F and access only to an approximation f whose error is uniformly at most ν. The proposed algorithm runs stochastic gradient descent on a smoothed version of f. It is guaranteed to find an ε-approximate local minimum of F when ν is at most O(ε^1.5/d), linking the allowable approximation error to accuracy and dimension.

An almost matching lower bound shows that this error tolerance is essentially optimal among algorithms using a polynomial number of queries to f. The authors also apply the result to derive sample complexities for learning a ReLU unit. The contribution explains when smoothing an accessible empirical objective can recover meaningful local solutions of an inaccessible population objective despite sampling-induced irregularities.
neurips-2018-on-the-local-minima-of-the-.tldr: SGD on a smoothed empirical objective can find population-risk local minima under an essentially optimal uniform approximation-error condition.

paragraphs: A latent-state linear dynamical system describes an evolving process through internal states that are not directly observed. Learning such a system raises the question of whether those internal dynamics must first be explicitly identified. This paper gives a polynomial-time learning algorithm that avoids system identification, broadening the ways these models can be learned efficiently.

The approach extends spectral filtering, a technique previously applied only when the system's transition matrix was symmetric. Its key technical addition is a convex relaxation that permits efficient identification of phases. That relaxation supplies the mechanism for moving beyond the earlier symmetry restriction while retaining a computationally tractable learning procedure.

The stated result also makes no assumption about the transition matrix's spectral radius. Together, removing the symmetry restriction and avoiding a spectral-radius assumption expand the scope of the spectral-filtering approach. The contribution is a theoretical algorithmic extension: it establishes efficient learning for more general latent-state linear dynamics without requiring explicit system identification as an intermediate step.
neurips-2018-spectral-filtering-for-gene.tldr: A convex relaxation extends spectral filtering to general latent-state linear systems without system identification or spectral-radius assumptions.

paragraphs: For smooth nonconvex objectives, reaching a point with little gradient does not by itself establish that the point is a local minimum; saddle points also matter. This paper proposes a stochastic version of the cubic-regularized Newton method designed to escape saddles efficiently and find approximate local minima.

The algorithm uses stochastic gradients and stochastic Hessian-vector products. A Hessian-vector product supplies curvature information along a direction, and the abstract states that these products can be computed as efficiently as stochastic gradients. This makes curvature information available through operations whose individual cost can remain comparable to the gradient computations already used in stochastic optimization.

The method requires Õ(ε^-3.5) evaluations of these quantities, improving on the stated Õ(ε^-4) rate for stochastic gradient descent. The notation suppresses logarithmic factors. Its rate matches the best-known local-minimum result cited in the abstract without delicate acceleration or variance-reduction techniques. The contribution is therefore a stronger evaluation-complexity guarantee for approximate local optimization, achieved through a stochastic curvature-based method.
neurips-2018-stochastic-cubic-regulariza.tldr: Stochastic cubic regularization finds approximate local minima with Õ(ε^-3.5) gradient and Hessian-vector evaluations, improving the stated SGD rate.

paragraphs: Editing an image from a text description requires changing the requested visual attributes while preserving content unrelated to the instruction. This paper addresses that selective editing problem. It observes that existing methods can create the desired new attributes but do not fully preserve the original image's text-irrelevant content.

The proposed Text-Adaptive Generative Adversarial Network uses a discriminator that changes with the input description. It creates local discriminators at the word level to evaluate fine-grained attributes independently. This gives the generator feedback tied to particular parts of the text, helping it learn to modify the corresponding image regions while retaining other content.

Experiments on CUB and Oxford-102 report improvements over existing methods, and participants in a user study mostly preferred the proposed method's outputs. Further analysis indicates that the model can separate visual attributes effectively and produce pleasing images. These findings support text-adaptive discrimination as a way to make language-guided editing more selective, with both comparative experiments and user judgments contributing evidence for the reported image quality.
neurips-2018-text-adaptive-generative-ad.tldr: TAGAN uses word-level, text-adaptive discriminators to edit requested image attributes while preserving unrelated content.

paragraphs: The retina divides visual information into parallel pathways carried by different ganglion-cell types. This paper asks why such diversity might be useful for efficient encoding of natural visual input. It studies naturalistic movies, so the information being encoded includes both spatial structure and changes over time, under a fixed firing-rate budget.

In a linear encoding model, the authors optimize the receptive fields and densities of two convolutional cell types. The resulting types match properties of primate midget and parasol cells, including spatial and temporal sensitivity, spacing, and relative abundance. The theory also accounts for how the midget-to-parasol ratio decreases farther from the center of the retina.

A nonlinear model with rectification again develops receptive fields resembling midget and parasol cells, now further divided into ON and OFF types. The findings offer an efficient-coding justification for four dominant primate retinal cell types, together comprising 70% of ganglion cells. This is a theoretical explanation supported by optimized encoding models, connecting the diversity of visual pathways to the demands of representing natural movies efficiently.
neurips-2018-the-emergence-of-multiple-r.tldr: Optimizing movie encoding under a firing-rate budget produces model cell types resembling the retina's dominant midget and parasol pathways.

paragraphs: Program translation helps move software from one programming language into another ecosystem. This paper builds on the observation that translation is modular: a subtree in a source program corresponds to a subtree in the target program. The authors design a neural network around that structural relationship, translating a source tree into a target tree.

The model includes an attention mechanism tailored to tree generation. When the decoder expands a nonterminal in the target tree, attention locates the corresponding source subtree and uses it to guide the expansion. This connects each local construction decision to relevant source structure, reflecting the paper's view of translation as a sequence of related subtree transformations.

Evaluation compares the model with other neural translation models and established program-translation approaches. The authors report consistent gains over neural baselines, with margins reaching 15 points, and a 20-point improvement over previous state-of-the-art approaches on real-world projects. These findings support preserving and attending to program structure as a useful design choice for the translation tasks evaluated.
neurips-2018-tree-to-tree-neural-network.tldr: A tree-to-tree network uses subtree attention to translate program structure and improves results over the evaluated translation approaches.

paragraphs: Video-to-video synthesis converts a source sequence, such as segmentation masks, into a photorealistic video depicting its content. Treating every frame as an independent image can produce poor visual quality and inconsistency over time. This paper addresses the need to model temporal dynamics as part of the synthesis process.

The proposed approach uses generative adversarial learning with carefully designed generators and discriminators and an objective that accounts for both space and time. It supports several source formats, including segmentation masks, sketches, and poses. The reported outputs combine high resolution, photorealism, and temporal coherence, addressing both the appearance of individual frames and their consistency as a sequence.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks show advantages over strong baselines. A highlighted capability is generating street-scene videos at 2K resolution for durations of up to 30 seconds. The authors also apply the method to future-video prediction and outperform several competing systems. These findings demonstrate the value of explicitly incorporating temporal behavior into adversarial synthesis across both source-conditioned generation and prediction.
neurips-2018-video-to-video-synthesis-3b.tldr: A spatiotemporal adversarial approach generates photorealistic, coherent videos from structured input sequences, including 2K street scenes.

paragraphs: Recognition depends partly on whether a model's learned features make classes easy to distinguish. Useful features should keep examples of the same class relatively compact while separating examples from different classes. This paper proposes Virtual Softmax, a simple modification to ordinary softmax training intended to encourage both properties.

The method introduces a dynamic virtual negative class into the original softmax. That extra class strengthens the constraint imposed by the decision boundary, aiming to enlarge the space between classes and tighten each class's feature distribution. The virtual class serves as part of the learning objective, providing additional pressure for features to become more compact and separable.

The authors explain the motivation for this modification and present empirical evidence of improved discrimination. Experiments report performance gains across a variety of object-classification and face-verification tasks. The findings suggest that a small change to the classification objective can improve the geometry of learned representations and benefit recognition, without requiring the central idea to be a more elaborate feature-learning mechanism.
neurips-2018-virtual-class-enhanced-disc.tldr: Virtual Softmax adds a dynamic negative class to encourage tighter within-class features and greater separation between classes.
